newsitem.title: FRANCE: Is is too late for Renault and Volvo?.
newsitem.headline: Is is too late for Renault and Volvo?.

text.p: The departure of Volvo managing director Soren Gyll, the chief opponent of a linkup with Renault, has stirred speculation that Renault and Volvo might have another go at it.
Such a prospect would have been unthinkable until recently, given the bitterness of the split three and a years ago after Swedish shareholders rebelled against a planned alliance.

But both companies are vulnerable in an increasingly global and cutthroat industry -- particularly in Europe, where competition will grow even fiercer as barriers against Asian imports come down in the year 2000.
The biggest obstacles to a merger have been removed. Renault is no longer state-controlled, and Gyll stepped down in January.

"The chairman that killed the agreement has left. The new chairman was not involved. The top management has been replaced, and both companies are thinking about what they should do," said a Paris-based car analyst. "It's clear they're negotiating."
Last month the Swedish newspaper Svenska Dagbladet said Renault and Volvo were discussing the possible sale of Renault's Mack Trucks to Volvo.

Although both companies denied the report, the scenario rang true. Volvo Trucks says it wants to double its North American market share to 20 percent, and the acquisition of Mack Trucks would achieve that overnight.

Although Mack is profitable, it is also under pressure to make a move following the acquisition in February of Ford Motor Co's truck business by industry leader Daimler-Benz AG's Freightliner subsidiary and the Paccar-DAF merger.
Analysts say it would not make sense for Renault to sell Mack after having spent a great deal of effort to develop synergies between the European and U.S. truck businesses.

But they say a deal involving the whole of the two companies' truck operations might be feasible because the European operations also have a good fit. Volvo is strong in northern Europe and Renault is the leader in France and Spain.
On the car side, Renault has the bigger operation with annual sales of 1.4 million cars, compared with Volvo's 375,000, but Volvo is more successful selling cars outside Europe.

"The analysis we made three years ago is still correct. The two companies' products are still complementary, and we would be stronger together," Renault's European sales director Philippe Gambas told Automotive News Europe.
"Even though we broke off our engagement three years ago, we could still marry," he added.
Pressure on Renault to act has also mounted since March when it reported a 5.25 billion franc ($903.8 million) loss for 1996.
Most share analysts doubt Volvo and Renault are interested in the sort of marriage they had in mind previously.

"I'd be astonished if a grand alliance was again on the agenda," said John Lawson at Salomon Brothers. He said the car businesses would not mix easily, given Volvo's concentration on the high end of the model range and its strong brand identity.
Production plans are too far along to allow for immediate cooperation in key cost-cutting areas such as platform-sharing, said Nigel Griffiths at DRI/McGraw Hill.
"Even if they kissed and made up today, it would be impossible to cooperate on the next launches," he said. "I don't see synergies occurring before 2004."

Analysts say Volvo may have other options. One is Chrysler, which wants to boost sales in Europe and has ties with Mitsubishi, Volvo's partner in the NedCar venture in the Netherlands. "Since Mitsubishi and Volvo also have a relationship, there's scope for a triad," one analyst said.

Another possibility is GM-controlled Saab. "Both are Swedish, so you'd overcome the Scandinavian bias which scuppered the Renault-Volvo relationship," he said. But their combined sales are still small, less than 600,000 units a year.
What looks to be real is Volvo's interest in Mack, but it remains to be seen whether Renault is keen.
Although its truck business, Renault VI, lost money in 1996 and is expected to lose money this year, chairman Louis Schweitzer has said repeatedly the business is not for sale.
He says one of Renault's strengths is that it makes both cars and trucks, which have different business cycles.
But analysts are not convinced by that logic.
"Renault VI needs Mack. But does Renault need Renault VI? That's not so clear," one analyst said.
A sale might be a good thing, said another analyst. "Renault cars needs cash." ($ = 5.809 French Francs)
